items.title: Philip Sidney and the Extreme (Dis)graces of the Parenthesis
items.description: Erasmus called them “little moons” and George Puttenham praised them as “figures of tolerable disorder” (if used not too often “nor too thick”). For Philip Sidney, they were simply indispensable. Florence Hazrat introduces us to the uncontested early modern king of brackets and to his romance Arcadia, which abruptly ends, like its author’s life, hanging on a parenthesis.

items.title: Veronese's Dogs
items.description: “Oh, if I could only pray”, Luther once said of his dog Tölpel, “the way this dog watches the meat”. items.title: “Worthless Idiot, Donkey Head”: Parodies of Pedantry on the Renaissance Stage

items.title: Louis Pope Gratacap, A Curator in Lost Worlds
items.description: Arguably the first work of fiction to feature a *Tyrannosaurus rex*, Louis Pope Gratacap’s *The New Northland* (1915) is at once kaleidoscopic, mischievous, fascinating — and exhausting. Richard Fallon explores this “lost world” novel, finding a work as interested in cutting-edge science as it was in paying dues to its generic precursors.

items.title: Animal, Vegetable, Lamb: The Zoophyte from Tartary
items.description: In the Middle Ages, rumours spread across Europe of a strange hybrid creature, half-animal, half-plant, known as the Vegetable Lamb of Tartary. A hoax based on fern rhizomes? A euphemism for culled fetal lambs? Or perhaps a medieval misapprehension of cotton? Thom Sliwowski traces the roots of this fabled zoophyte.
